Most of my clients live in a different time zone than I do.
Jakarta, Berlin, New York, Sydney. For a long time my “system” was a world clock, a to-do app, a spreadsheet for hours and a separate tool for invoices. I kept asking myself the same question every day: what time is it for my client right now, and when should I send this?
So I built the tool I wanted. Meet Taskly  😊 
Under the hood: React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind and Supabase, deployed on Cloudflare. It works offline first, syncs in real time across devices, and every table is protected with Row Level Security.
What I learned: the hardest part of remote freelancing isn’t the work itself. It’s the coordination around it. Good tools should quietly remove that friction.
If you work with clients across time zones, I’d love your feedback. What is the one thing that slows you down the most?

Malaysia’s Data Centre Competitiveness: Limited Locations and Rising Operating Costs Pose Challenges.

Malaysia’s ambition to become a regional data centre hub could face growing challenges as limited development locations, rising operating costs and infrastructure constraints threaten its competitiveness against regional markets such as Thailand and Indonesia.

Speaking at Bursa Malaysia’s Sectorial Series, Powering the AI Era — Watt Next?, industry representatives highlighted Malaysia’s relatively concentrated data centre ecosystem, with most developments located in Johor. This contrasts with Thailand, which offers developers greater flexibility in selecting power providers, and Indonesia, which has a wider geographical distribution of potential development sites.

Malaysia’s key constraints include electricity and water availability, suitable land, infrastructure capacity and the geographical distance between potential locations. These factors could increase development and operating costs while limiting the pace at which new data centre projects can be established.

Greater Kuala Lumpur remains attractive due to its established infrastructure and connectivity, while Johor continues to serve as the country's principal data centre development hub. Northern states could provide additional opportunities to diversify the geographical distribution of future investments. However, network latency — the time required for data to travel between locations — remains an important consideration.

According to TM Global's General Manager of Data Centre Architecture and Delivery, Isaac Goh, latency requirements vary depending on the intended applications. A range of seven to nine milliseconds may be acceptable for certain workloads, including AI training, whereas AI inference typically requires lower latency of approximately five to six milliseconds. Consequently, not every location will be suitable for every type of data centre operation.

The Strategic Implication
Malaysia must move beyond attracting data centre investments through incentives and market positioning alone. Long-term competitiveness will depend on reliable and affordable electricity, sustainable water supply, robust telecommunications infrastructure, suitable land availability and efficient regulatory approvals.

Expanding development opportunities beyond Johor and Greater Kuala Lumpur could strengthen national resilience, encourage regional economic participation and reduce geographical concentration risks. However, site diversification must be supported by adequate power infrastructure, fibre connectivity and application-specific latency requirements.

From Indonesia and the Philippines to Malaysia, countries across the ASEAN region are advancing carbon markets. Ensuring these systems are transparent and trusted will be key for investor confidence.

At #COP31 speakers from across the region alongside global experts, shared their insights on how governments can build effective and successful carbon markets.

Across Southeast Asia, projects are already under way. In the Philippines, last month the President signed an executive order directing the country to develop a national carbon market framework. In Indonesia, a new regulation on carbon pricing was introduced just last year, opening up opportunities for carbon markets. Meanwhile, in April, Malaysia launched its National Carbon Market Policy. 

Nani Hendiarti,Coordinating Ministry for Food Affairs of the Republic of Indonesia shared how the country’s carbon market registry and infrastructure is being implemented, while also calling for stronger collaborations across the ASEAN region. She noted a need to have interoperability between national systems and the international standard and shared that, “we need to get the high integrity…the goal is actually to get the transparency and traceability and also the trust.”

In the Philippines,Sandee Recabar, Department of Environment and Natural Resources explained how, as projects are being implemented, this could work in practice sharing,  “it's very important for the project developers to monitor at what stage are their projects now in terms of the approval process. So we're trying to design that system for that.”

Fundamentally, monitoring, reporting, and verification (MRV) systems provide the emissions data and assurance that carbon pricing systems rely on to operate credibly. The success of these systems, however, depends on inclusive design and governance. This means tracking whose voices shape MRV rules in the first place and whether affected workers and communities can meaningfully take part. IISD'sPhilip Gass emphasized: “Is there work development opportunities? Is there employment? Are people that are impacted…seeing benefits from the project and from the revenues that are being raised as well…those value-added benefits of social inclusion, gender equity, and that's how you get the premiums on the projects you're developing as well.”

“Integrity and quality is really something that we do not want to compromise on. Because at the end of the day, what we are building here in ASEAN, right, is actually a trust infrastructure, and we really have to make sure that we are all aligned and, and we are all on the same page,”Dr Renard Siew, Malaysia Carbon Market Association.

#AI #NewWorld
1. DataCamp
Recommendation #1 from me. From data analyst, scientist, engineer, to LLM, everything is covered in detail, including video explanations, coding practice, certification, and training projects. For you students, you can use GitHub Edu to get certificates and access several AI and data science learning courses.

2. Kaggle
Through this free website, the material is more complete than what you get in IT college. The dataset is abundant, complete with sample notebook code. You can also take practice-based courses; here you will learn by doing. You can also join competitions to earn extra pocket money.

3. Codecademy
In Indonesia, it seems less well known compared to others. I used to buy a sharing account to access projects here, and the point I liked was that it was interactive and project-based. Even so, there are still many free courses for those of you who want to learn from the basics.

4. Coursera
The material is complete and the roadmap is structured, but the downside is that the course takes a long time and is too theory-based. Not for everyone, but it is very suitable for beginners who are new to IT.

5. YouTube
There are many channels to learn fundamental technical tools, such as Krish Naik, 3Blue1Brown, AI Engineer, Data Lumina. The information is up to date, with shortcomings that are less structured. It is more suitable to be alternated with joining competitions or studying in other courses.

6. Udemy
Just like YouTube, it's good because the material is diverse and there are many very specific course options. You can find courses for almost any topic, from fundamentals to fairly advanced material. But it can't be relied upon alone. It needs to be accompanied by hands-on projects on GitHub, creating side projects, and other hands-on practice.

7. LinkedIn learning
The course is short and easy to complete, suitable for those who don't have free time but still want to improve their skills; However, the technical depth is minimal, making it more suitable as an initial step in introducing material within the work environment.

8. freeCodeCamp
This is good for software engineers and fundamentals, the community is large, unfortunately the website doesn't have an up-to-date roadmap to study data science and AI specializations. I would recommend watching it on YouTube.

This is a subjective assessment of my personal experience that I have tried everything. There are many courses in Indonesian, such as dicoding, myskills, hacktiv, but personally I prefer learning from English-language and foreign sources. Besides learning English, the overseas curriculum for AI and data science, in my opinion, is more complete and up to date

"Can you run a coaching refresher training for our leaders?"

I've heard this request from HR teams more than once. Their concern was the same: leaders had been trained as coaches, but in practice, coaching wasn't being done the way it should.

So I went in to find out why.

What I found surprised me. The leaders weren't unwilling. They knew the principles. Some even had coaching sessions on their calendar.

But when targets pressed and a crisis came up, they slipped back into command and control. The coaching session became an instruction session. In that moment, they forgot they were people developers, and that developing people is an investment, not a distraction.

And because the impact of coaching was never measured, it slowly looked like coaching "didn't work."

A refresher wouldn't fix that. Leaders didn't need to relearn coaching. They needed to make it a habit, go deeper in their skills, and see its impact on the numbers.

We are looking for a Senior Database Specialist with 5+ years of experience, particularly in SQL Server to PostgreSQL Migration | Project Duration: 12 months | Work Location: Onsite – North Jakarta

Experience & Seniority
Minimum of 7+ years of experience as a Database Engineer, Database Administrator (DBA), or Database Consultant, including at least 3 years of hands-on experience managing cross-engine database migration projects.
Proven experience leading at least one large-scale (multi-terabyte) SQL Server to PostgreSQL migration project, successfully completed through go-live and post-migration stabilization.
Cross-Database Engine Expertise
Microsoft SQL Server / Azure SQL: Strong proficiency in T-SQL, execution plans, Change Tracking/CDC, and understanding of Azure SQL Database (PaaS) configurations and limitations.
PostgreSQL / Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL: Strong expertise in query planning and optimization, indexing strategies (B-tree, partial, covering, GIN/GiST as appropriate), VACUUM/ANALYZE, statistics management, and parameter tuning.
Ability to identify and map behavioral differences between database engines, including data types, isolation levels, collation, date/time functions, and NULL handling.
AWS Ecosystem
- Solid understanding of Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL, RDS Proxy (connection multiplexing and pinning), Amazon EKS, CloudWatch, Performance Insights / Database Insights, and AWS Secrets Manager / IAM authentication in database environments.
Application Layer Understanding
Working knowledge of .NET / .NET Core applications using Entity Framework Core and Npgsql, sufficient to diagnose ORM-generated query patterns and recommend improvements (projection, batching, connection pooling, No Reset On Close, etc.).
Candidates are not required to be .NET developers but must be able to understand and bridge the interaction between application-layer behavior and database performance.
Communication & Language Skills
- Ability to communicate technical concepts clearly in both Bahasa Indonesia and English 
(spoken and written), effectively engaging with both technical and managerial stakeholders.

Additional Qualifications (Nice-to-Have)
AWS certifications, such as AWS Certified Database – Specialty orAWS Certified Solutions Architect.
Experience with Aurora Query Plan Management (apg_plan_mgmt/QPM) and advanced optimizer flags.
Experience optimizing heavy batch and OLTP workloads, such as end-of-day (EOD) or close-of-business (COB) processing.
Relevant industry experience in banking, automotive, or enterprise environments, with an understanding of regulatory compliance and data security requirements.
Understanding ofZero-ETL strategies, data warehousing, and cross-region Disaster Recovery (DR) in Amazon Aurora environments.

Interested candidates can apply directly through this post or send their updated CV to:dian.maharani@prointegrate.net | Feel free to share this opportunity with your network!
